title: Al-Ghazali Versus Ibn Rushd
objective: After this level you can explain the debate between al-Ghazali's Incoherence of the Philosophers and Ibn Rushd's reply, including their dispute over fire burning cotton.
summary: Al-Ghazali argued that observation shows only fire and burning together, not a necessary link; Ibn Rushd replied that fire really burns and that denying causes denies knowledge.

cards.headline: Does fire really burn cotton?
cards.body: Obviously, you’d say. Hold a flame to a cotton ball and it catches. One of the most influential thinkers of Sunni Islam argued that you have never actually seen the fire do it.

cards.headline: The Incoherence of the Philosophers
cards.body: Al-Ghazali, who died in 1111, took aim at philosophers such as Avicenna in his book The Incoherence of the Philosophers. He examined twenty of their teachings. His main charge wasn’t that all of them were false, but that their arguments fell short of the strict proof the philosophers themselves demanded. His longest discussion attacks their claim that the world has always existed.

cards.headline: You only ever see them together
cards.body: His famous example: fire touches cotton, and the cotton burns. Observation, al-Ghazali argued, shows only that the burning happens together with the touch, not that it happens through it. The link isn’t necessary: you can conceive of fire touching cotton without burning it. On one account he offered, God creates the burning each time, following a habit, and the fire itself does nothing.

cards.headline: The Incoherence of the Incoherence
cards.body: The philosopher and physician Ibn Rushd of Cordoba (Averroes, 1126 to 1198) answered with a book titled The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Fire keeps its power to burn, he argued, even if something like talc can block it. Every event has four causes: agent, form, matter and end. And to deny causes is to deny knowledge, since understanding a thing means grasping its causes.

cards.headline: Al-Ghazali Versus Ibn Rushd: the big picture
learned: Fire and cotton: we see them together, not a necessary link
Ibn Rushd: fire really burns, though talc can block it
Deny causes and you deny knowledge

questions.prompt: Put these thinkers from the Islamic world in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Avicenna died in 1037, al-Ghazali died in 1111, and Ibn Rushd lived from 1126 to 1198.

questions.prompt: Why did al-Ghazali say that watching fire and cotton can’t prove the fire causes the burning?

options.label: Fire burns too quickly for anyone to watch closely
options.rationale: The problem isn’t speed or heat.

options.label: Cotton never actually burns when fire touches it
options.rationale: It does burn; the question is why.

options.label: It shows them happening together, not a necessary link
Scholars of his time weren’t allowed to observe nature
options.rationale: He appeals to what observation shows.

questions.explanation: Observation shows the burning together with the touch; it can’t show a necessary link, since fire without burning is conceivable.

questions.prompt: Ibn Rushd defended causes with an older list of four. Which list?

options.label: Aristotle’s four causes: agent, form, matter, end
Nyaya’s four means of knowledge, including inference
options.rationale: That list is about how we know, not about causes.

options.label: Plato’s Forms of Beauty, Justice and Equality
Confucius’s virtues of ren and li, humaneness and ritual
options.rationale: Those are Confucian virtues, not causes.

questions.explanation: Ibn Rushd said every event has four causes, agent, form, matter and end: Aristotle’s efficient, formal, material and final causes.
